title: Digital nerve block and local anaesthetic safety

guidelineVersions: Association of Anaesthetists QRH 3-10, local anaesthetic toxicity (June 2023)

related.why: Closing the wound once the block works

brief.setting: Emergency department, minor injuries; on a hand model
brief.scenario: Mr Joel Mowbray, 29, a joiner, cut the back of his left middle finger over the proximal phalanx on a metal edge an hour ago. The clean 2 cm laceration needs suturing. He is fit, weighs 80 kg and takes no medicines. Plain lidocaine 1%, lidocaine 1% with adrenaline, 25-gauge needles, syringes, skin preparation and a sharps bin are provided.
brief.task: Perform a digital nerve block on the hand model, talking the examiner through each step, and answer questions on local anaesthetic safety.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Examine the finger first, choose plain lidocaine, know the dose limit, block both sides, wait, test, watch for toxicity.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Picking up the lidocaine with adrenaline, or blocking before testing sensation.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Before any anaesthetic, I'll test sensation on both sides of the finger and the tendons."

grid.label: Consent and pre-procedure checks
grid.fail: Starts without consent or asking about allergies.
grid.pass: Confirms identity, explains the block, and asks about local anaesthetic allergy, anticoagulants and weight; gains consent.
grid.high: Knows an amide allergy rules out lidocaine and bupivacaine, and checks resuscitation equipment is at hand.

grid.label: Pre-block neurovascular exam (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Blocks the finger before testing sensation or tendons.
grid.pass: Before injecting: sensation both sides and dorsally distal to the wound; extension against resistance; flexion; capillary refill; records it.
grid.high: Uses two-point discrimination (over 6 mm static abnormal) and resisted PIP extension; suspected nerve or tendon injury goes to the hand team.

grid.label: Choice of anaesthetic (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Uses lidocaine with adrenaline in the finger.
grid.pass: Chooses plain lidocaine 1%; states adrenaline is contraindicated in fingers under the UK product licence.
grid.high: Knows the evidence debate over adrenaline in digits, but follows the UK SmPC.

grid.label: Maximum dose
grid.borderline: Knows a limit exists but quotes the 500 mg with-adrenaline figure.
grid.pass: Plain lidocaine: 4.5 mg/kg up to 200 mg; for 80 kg the limit is 200 mg, 20 ml of 1%.
grid.high: Uses a small fraction of it; would reduce the dose in the elderly or debilitated.

grid.label: Anatomy and technique
grid.fail: Injects only one side of the finger.
grid.pass: Two dorsal and two palmar digital nerves; fine needle at the finger base, dorsal then palmar on each side; aspirates first.
grid.high: Explains the dorsal approach suits this dorsal wound; it anaesthetises the back of the finger better than a single palmar injection.

grid.label: Asepsis and sharps
grid.fail: Recaps the needle or leaves it on the tray.
grid.pass: Cleans the skin, wears gloves, disposes of the needle straight into the sharps bin.
grid.high: Never recaps; knows a needlestick needs first aid, reporting and urgent occupational health advice.

grid.label: Onset, testing and documentation
grid.fail: Starts suturing straight away without testing.
grid.pass: Waits for the block to work and tests sensation before starting; documents drug, dose and time.
grid.high: If still sensate, waits longer before giving more; records the pre-block examination alongside the dose.

grid.label: Local anaesthetic toxicity (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Can't name the warning signs, or keeps injecting.
grid.pass: Signs: circumoral tingling, tinnitus, confusion, seizures, arrhythmias; stops injecting, calls for help, ABC, oxygen, IV access.
grid.high: 20% lipid emulsion: 1.5 ml/kg over 2–3 minutes, then 15 ml/kg/h; toxicity can occur some time after the injection.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Starts drawing up without asking about allergies or consent.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'll use the lidocaine with adrenaline; it'll stop the bleeding.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'm not sure, but it's a small amount.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He says his lips are tingling.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mr Mowbray, can I check your name and date of birth? I'd like to numb the finger with injections at its base. Any allergy to local anaesthetic? Blood thinners? You're 80 kg? Happy to go ahead?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Tests light touch on both sides of the finger and on the back beyond the wound, extension against resistance, flexion at each joint, and capillary refill.] All normal; I'll record that.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Plain lidocaine 1%. Adrenaline is contraindicated in fingers in the UK product information.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The maximum is 4.5 mg/kg up to 200 mg, so 200 mg for him, 20 ml of 1%. I'll need far less.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Cleans the skin, gloves.] Each finger has two dorsal and two palmar nerves. [25-gauge needle at the base, dorsolaterally; aspirates, injects over the dorsal nerve, then advances towards the palmar side and injects; repeats on the other side.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Puts the needle straight into the sharps bin.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'll wait a few minutes and test before I start. I'll record the drug, dose and time.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: He says his lips are tingling.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That could be toxicity. I'll stop injecting, call for help, check airway, breathing and circulation, give oxygen and get IV access.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Can I confirm your name and date of birth? I'll numb the finger at its base. Any allergy to local anaesthetic? If you'd reacted to lidocaine, bupivacaine is no alternative; both are amides. Blood thinners? 80 kg? [Checks the resuscitation trolley is nearby.] Happy to go ahead?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Two-point discrimination with a paper clip on each side, 4 mm; light touch on the back beyond the wound; PIP extension against resistance; flexion; capillary refill.] Normal. Over 6 mm, or weak extension, would mean a nerve or tendon injury for the hand team.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Plain lidocaine 1%. There's evidence adrenaline may be safe in fingers, but the UK SmPC contraindicates it, so I won't use it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: His limit is 200 mg, the lower of 4.5 mg/kg and 200 mg. I'll use a small fraction of that, and less again in someone frail.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [25-gauge needle each side at the base; aspirates; dorsal nerve, then palmar.] The dorsal approach suits a wound on the back of the finger; it numbs the back better than a single palmar injection.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Needle straight into the sharps bin; no recapping.] If I had a needlestick: first aid, report it, occupational health urgently.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Plain lidocaine usually works within a few minutes; then I'll test both sides. If he can still feel it, I'll wait longer before adding more. I'll record the pre-block exam, drug, dose and time.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He says his lips are tingling and his ears are ringing.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Possible toxicity: stop, call for help, airway, oxygen, IV access, monitor. If it's severe, 20% lipid emulsion, 1.5 ml/kg over 2 to 3 minutes, then 15 ml/kg an hour. It can come on late, so I'd observe him.

failures.move: Using lidocaine with adrenaline for a digital block.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: contrary to the UK SmPC, which contraindicates vasoconstrictors in fingers.

failures.move: Blocking before testing sensation and tendon function.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: a digital nerve injury can no longer be detected, and may be missed.

failures.move: Continuing to inject when he reports tingling lips.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: systemic toxicity can progress to seizures and cardiac arrest.

failures.move: Blocking only one side of the finger.
failures.consequence: Half the finger stays sensate, so he feels the repair and more anaesthetic is given.

recovery.when: You picked up the adrenaline vial
recovery.line: Sorry, that's lidocaine with adrenaline. For a finger I'll use plain lidocaine.

recovery.when: You forgot to test sensation first
recovery.line: Before I inject, I need to test sensation and tendons and record them.

knowledge.fact: Each finger has paired palmar and dorsal digital nerves, running along each side.
Plain lidocaine: single dose no more than 4.5 mg/kg or 200 mg in adults.
With adrenaline: maximum 500 mg; vasoconstrictors contraindicated in fingers, toes, nose tip, ears and penis.
A Cochrane review (4 RCTs) found no reported distal ischaemia with adrenaline, but judged the evidence insufficient to recommend use or avoidance; the UK licence still contraindicates it.
Bupivacaine: single dose up to 150 mg; no more than 2 mg/kg in any 4 hours.
Two-point discrimination over 6 mm static or 4 mm moving is abnormal.
Severe toxicity: stop injecting, call for help, airway, oxygen, IV access; 20% lipid 1.5 ml/kg over 2–3 minutes, then 15 ml/kg/h.
Plain lidocaine digital blocks: mean onset about 3 minutes, duration about 2 hours.

recall.think: Test first, plain drug, stay under the limit.
recall.say: "Plain lidocaine: adrenaline is contraindicated in fingers in the UK."
do: Both sides, dorsal then palmar; aspirate

numbers.meaning: 1% plain lidocaine at the 200 mg limit

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; introduce yourself, explain the task, confirm identity and obtain consent at every station

sources.name: Lidocaine Hydrochloride Injection BP 1% w/v (hameln): Summary of Product Characteristics (emc 6277)
sources.version: Date of revision of the text 4 February 2022
sources.supports: Local anaesthesia: single doses (other than spinal) should not exceed 4.5 mg/kg (or 200 mg) in adults; doses generally reduced in children, the elderly or debilitated (4.2); contraindicated with hypersensitivity to amide local anaesthetics (4.3); resuscitation facilities should be available (4.4); signs of systemic toxicity: dizziness, circumoral paraesthesia, tongue numbness, tinnitus, drowsiness, convulsions, coma; hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias and cardiac arrest (4.8)

sources.name: Lidocaine 1% with adrenaline 1:200,000 solution for injection: Summary of Product Characteristics (emc 2397)
sources.supports: Maximum single dose of lidocaine given with adrenaline 500 mg (4.2); careful aspiration before and during injection (4.4); the use of a vasoconstrictor is contraindicated for anaesthesia of fingers, toes, tip of nose, ears and penis

sources.name: Bupivacaine 5 mg/ml solution for injection (Baxter): Summary of Product Characteristics (emc 11612)
sources.version: Date of revision of the text 31 January 2024
sources.supports: Single dose up to 150 mg; a maximum of 2 mg/kg should not be exceeded in any four-hour period (4.2)

sources.name: RCEMLearning reference: Soft tissue injuries of the hand (Dorani B; eds Sloan JP, Mahony KL)
sources.supports: Two-point discrimination is the most reliable sensory test in the hand; a paper clip is usually adequate; more than 6 mm static or 4 mm moving is abnormal; early recognition of nerve injury matters because primary repair is superior to delayed repair

sources.name: Association of Anaesthetists: Quick Reference Handbook (QRH), guideline 3-10 Local anaesthetic toxicity (v.2; replaces the withdrawn AAGBI 2010 laminate)
sources.supports: Signs of severe toxicity: sudden alteration in mental status, severe agitation or loss of consciousness, with or without convulsions; cardiovascular collapse; may occur some time after the initial injection; stop injecting, call for help, 100% oxygen and adequate ventilation, IV access; control seizures (small incremental benzodiazepine first); in circulatory arrest, CPR with a smaller adrenaline dose (1 microgram/kg or less) and no vasopressin; 20% lipid emulsion: 1.5 ml/kg over 2-3 minutes, then 15 ml/kg/h; repeat bolus at 5 and 10 minutes and double the rate to 30 ml/kg/h if cardiovascular stability is not restored; maximum cumulative 12 ml/kg; propofol is not a substitute

sources.name: Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013 (SI 2013/645)
sources.supports: Employers must ensure needles are not capped after use unless a risk assessment requires it and a suitable device controls the risk, and that secure sharps containers are close to where sharps are used (reg 5(1)); after a sharps injury with possible exposure, immediate medical advice and any post-exposure prophylaxis (reg 7(2))

sources.name: Gray's Anatomy for Students (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell)
sources.supports: Digital nerves of the hand: palmar digital nerves from the median and ulnar nerves and dorsal digital nerves from the radial and ulnar nerves, running along each side of the digit

sources.name: Clement P, et al. Regional anaesthesia on the finger: traditional dorsal digital nerve block versus subcutaneous volar nerve block, a randomized controlled trial. Injury 2021;52(4):883-888
sources.supports: In 409 adults, the traditional two-injection dorsal digital block anaesthetised the dorsal side of the finger better than a single subcutaneous volar injection, and is preferred for dorsal injuries; injection discomfort did not differ

sources.name: Vinycomb TI, et al. Comparison of local anesthetics for digital nerve blocks: a systematic review. J Hand Surg Am 2014;39(4):744-751.e5
sources.supports: Six studies (335 digital blocks): plain lidocaine had the shortest mean onset (3.1 minutes) and shortest mean duration (1.8 hours)

sources.name: Prabhakar H, et al. Adrenaline with lidocaine for digital nerve blocks. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(3):CD010645
sources.supports: Four RCTs, 167 participants, low-quality evidence: no trial reported ischaemia distal to the injection site; evidence insufficient to recommend use or avoidance of adrenaline in digital nerve blocks

partner.opening: Please perform a digital nerve block on this hand model for Mr Mowbray, talking me through what you're doing.

reveals.trigger: Asks about allergies, medicines and weight
reveals.finding: No allergies, no anticoagulants, 80 kg. He agrees to the block.

reveals.trigger: Examines the finger before the block
reveals.finding: Two-point discrimination 4 mm on both sides; normal light touch on the back of the finger beyond the wound; strong extension against resistance, including at the PIP joint; full flexion; capillary refill under 2 seconds.
At 5 minutes: "Still a bit of feeling on the thumb side." At 10 minutes: "Numb now."

push.question: Why not use the lidocaine with adrenaline?
push.expect: The UK SmPC contraindicates vasoconstrictors in fingers, toes, nose tip, ears and penis.

push.question: What is the maximum dose for him?
push.expect: Plain lidocaine 4.5 mg/kg up to 200 mg: 200 mg, 20 ml of 1%.

push.question: How would you recognise and treat toxicity?
push.expect: Circumoral tingling, tinnitus, confusion, seizures, arrhythmias; stop, call for help, ABC, oxygen, IV access; 20% lipid emulsion for severe toxicity.

curveballs.prompt: The nurse says only lidocaine with adrenaline is open.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Decline it and open plain lidocaine; it is contraindicated in fingers.

curveballs.prompt: He tells you he had a reaction to lidocaine at the dentist.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Don't give an amide such as lidocaine or bupivacaine; discuss alternatives with a senior.

curveballs.prompt: Before the block, two-point discrimination is 10 mm on the radial side.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Possible digital nerve injury: record it, and refer to the hand team rather than simply closing.

curveballs.prompt: After the injection he becomes confused and twitchy.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Treat as toxicity: stop, call for help, ABC, oxygen, IV access, control seizures, and give 20% lipid emulsion per the guideline.
